title: Finite Taylor jets of holomorphic germs
statement:
For an integer $d\geq0$, let $G_d$ be the commutative $\mathbf C$-algebra of germs at $0\in\mathbf C^d$ of holomorphic complex-valued functions: representatives are functions on open neighbourhoods of $0$, and two representatives agree when they agree on some smaller open neighbourhood. Holomorphic means locally representable by a convergent complex power series; operations and scalar multiplication are pointwise [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations]. Let $z_i\in G_d$ be the coordinate germs, let $\mathfrak q=\{g\in G_d:g(0)=0\}$, and let $P_d=\mathbf C[T_1,\ldots,T_d]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] with $J=(T_1,\ldots,T_d)$. Then $\mathfrak q=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)$, and, for every integer $r\geq1$, polynomial evaluation $T_i\mapsto z_i$ induces an isomorphism of $\mathbf C$-algebras
$$e_r:P_d/J^r\xrightarrow{\sim}G_d/\mathfrak q^r.$$
Its inverse sends the class of $g$ to the class of its Taylor polynomial $\sum_{|\alpha|<r}(\partial^\alpha g)(0)T^\alpha/\alpha!$, where $\alpha\in\mathbf N^d$, $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$ and $\partial^\alpha$ is the iterated coordinate derivative. The maps $e_r$ commute with reduction from exponent $r+1$ to $r$. For $d=0$, $G_0=P_0=\mathbf C$ and both ideals are zero.

source.place: WANTED locally. Serre GAGA no.4, printed p.6, holomorphic germs identified with convergent series, and no.6 Proposition 3, printed p.10, affine-space completion calculation. Finite-jet formulation is the Taylor-truncation refinement of that calculation; read online https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1956__6__1_0.pdf. Also Frenkel, Cartan seminar 1951-52 exp.10, sections 1 and 4 (convergent-series ring).

proof.text: If $d=0$, the space $\mathbf C^0$ is a singleton, so a germ is exactly its value in $\mathbf C$. The polynomial definition gives $P_0=\mathbf C$ because the only monomial is $1$. Thus $\mathfrak q=J=0$, every $e_r$ is the identity, and the Taylor polynomial has only its constant term. Henceforth assume $d>0$.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1956__6__1_0.pdf, no.4 printed p.6 and no.6 Proposition 3 affine-space case printed p.10. Agent-written finite-jet refinement using the existing coordinate-division and analytic-calculus nodes.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-holomorphic-coordinate-division] with its number of normal variables equal to $d$ and its number of parameter variables equal to $0$. For every $g\in G_d$ it gives $g-g(0)=\sum_{i=1}^d z_i h_i$ with $h_i\in G_d$. Each $z_i$ vanishes at zero, and every multiple and finite sum of such germs does too. Conversely, if $g(0)=0$, the displayed equality puts $g$ in $(z_1,\ldots,z_d)$. This proves $\mathfrak q=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)$.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1956__6__1_0.pdf, no.4 printed p.6 and no.6 Proposition 3 affine-space case printed p.10. Agent-written finite-jet refinement using the existing coordinate-division and analytic-calculus nodes.

proof.text: Iterate that same division finitely. For a word $w=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)\in\{1,\ldots,d\}^k$, put $z_w=z_{i_1}\cdots z_{i_k}$. Induct on $k\geq1$ to obtain $g=p_k(z)+\sum_{|w|=k}z_w h_w$, where $p_k\in P_d$ has only monomials of total degree less than $k$. The base is step 2 with $p_1=g(0)$. For the induction step write $h_w=h_w(0)+\sum_i z_i h_{w,i}$ by [lem-sfb-holomorphic-coordinate-division], and set $p_{k+1}=p_k+\sum_{|w|=k}h_w(0)T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k}$. The new remainder is $\sum_{w,i}z_wz_i h_{w,i}$, as required. All sums are finite. In particular $g-p_r(z)\in\mathfrak q^r$.

proof.text: Coordinate derivatives of germs are well-defined: equal representatives on an open neighbourhood have the same difference quotients and hence derivatives there. The first clause of [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-inverse-toolkit] supplies a strict derivative for each analytic representative at each point; setting the second point equal to the base point in its defining estimate gives the ordinary derivative. By [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-derivative-rules] this derivative is analytic on the open domain. Evaluation of a continuous linear map at a fixed coordinate vector is continuous complex-linear, so [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations] makes each coordinate derivative analytic too. Repetition therefore permits all finite ordered coordinate derivatives. Their sum and product rules and $\partial_i z_j=\delta_{ij}$ follow from [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-derivative-rules].

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1956__6__1_0.pdf, no.4 printed p.6 and no.6 Proposition 3 affine-space case printed p.10. Agent-written finite-jet refinement using the existing coordinate-division and analytic-calculus nodes.

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in\mathbf N^d$ and apply $\alpha_i$ derivatives in coordinate $i$, in a fixed coordinate order. Repeatedly applying the preceding product rule to $z_w h$, with $|w|=r$, gives terms in which $|\alpha|$ derivatives are distributed among the $r$ coordinate factors and $h$. If $|\alpha|<r$, some coordinate factor is undifferentiated in each term, so every term vanishes at zero. Step 2 and the definition of an ideal product express every element of $\mathfrak q^r$ as a finite sum of such $z_w h$: expand the $r$ factors from $\mathfrak q$ using their coordinate expressions. Thus $\partial^\alpha u(0)=0$ for $u\in\mathfrak q^r$ and $|\alpha|<r$. For a monomial $z^\beta$, the same rules give $\partial^\alpha z^\beta(0)=\alpha!$ if $\beta=\alpha$ and $0$ otherwise. Applying this to step 3 gives $[T^\alpha]p_r=\partial^\alpha g(0)/\alpha!$ for $|\alpha|<r$; the factorial is nonzero in $\mathbf C$.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1956__6__1_0.pdf, no.4 printed p.6 and no.6 Proposition 3 affine-space case printed p.10. Agent-written finite-jet refinement using the existing coordinate-division and analytic-calculus nodes.

proof.text: From the finite-monomial definition [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], every polynomial $p$ is its sum of monomials of degrees less than $r$ plus its sum of monomials of degrees at least $r$. Every high-degree monomial is divisible by a product of $r$ variables: choose $r$ occurrences from its total list of variable factors. Hence the high-degree part lies in $J^r$. Conversely, expanding a product of $r$ elements of $J$ gives only monomials of degree at least $r$, since each factor is a sum of variable multiples. Thus $p\in J^r$ exactly when all its coefficients in degrees less than $r$ vanish. In particular every class modulo $J^r$ has a unique representative supported in degrees less than $r$.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1956__6__1_0.pdf, no.4 printed p.6 and no.6 Proposition 3 affine-space case printed p.10. Agent-written finite-jet refinement using the existing coordinate-division and analytic-calculus nodes.

proof.text: The polynomial universal property [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] gives the $\mathbf C$-algebra map $e:p\mapsto p(z)$. Step 2 implies $e(J^r)\subseteq\mathfrak q^r$, so $[p]\mapsto[e(p)]$ is well-defined and preserves all algebra operations. Step 3 proves surjectivity. If $e(p)\in\mathfrak q^r$, step 5 gives $\alpha![T^\alpha]p=0$ for every $|\alpha|<r$; step 6 then gives $p\in J^r$. Hence the induced map is injective as well. Its inverse preserves the algebra operations because the bijection does. By steps 3 and 5 its inverse on $[g]$ is precisely the asserted Taylor polynomial class. If $g$ changes by an element of $\mathfrak q^r$, step 5 shows every coefficient used in this formula is unchanged, proving explicitly that the inverse formula is independent of the germ representative and the quotient representative.

proof.text: Reduction from exponent $r+1$ to $r$ sends $[p]$ to $[p]$ on the polynomial side and $[g]$ to $[g]$ on the germ side. Each composite in the desired square therefore sends $[p]$ to $[p(z)]$ modulo $\mathfrak q^r$, so the square commutes. Equivalently the Taylor polynomials at the two levels differ only by degree-$r$ monomials, which lie in $J^r$ by step 6.
